I kept telling myself I'd take two weeks off.

But I couldn't pull the trigger.

First, it was after this project wrapped up.

Then, after the next launch.

Then, after I hit the next revenue milestone.

The milestones kept moving.

And I kept working.

A few months ago, my wife just booked flights to Tokyo and put it on the calendar.

No asking. 
No waiting for the "right time."

She knew what I didn't: The right time never comes.

I automated everything before we left.

Newsletters scheduled. 
Social content queued. 
Systems running.

But I still had this nagging thought:

What if stepping away costs me momentum?

Here's what actually happened:

Revenue up 7% when I got back.

Every system ran fine.

And something else shifted that I didn't see coming.

The two weeks I spent not working did more for my business than the previous two months.

Not because I "recharged my batteries" or whatever people say.

But because I'd been running one mode nonstop for so long that I forgot other parts of me existed.

The parts that actually make the work better.

Most people think rest is the opposite of productivity.

It's not.

It's a different kind of fuel.

And when you finally give it space, something interesting happens to your output.

I'll break down exactly what shifted in tomorrow's newsletter, and why scheduling rest like you schedule work might be the highest-leverage move you're not making.

During World War II, analysts mapped bullet holes on planes that made it home. The pattern seemed obvious: reinforce the wings, tail, and fuselage—the places riddled with damage. A young statistician named Abraham Wald looked at the same dots and reached the opposite conclusion. He asked one question that changed everything: What about the planes that never returned? The answer was hiding in plain sight. The quiet areas on the survivors—engines, fuel systems, pilot area—that's where damage had been fatal. The military followed his logic and survival rates improved.

That's Survivorship Bias in one story: We focus on visible successes, ignore invisible failures, and draw entirely wrong conclusions. You see it everywhere. We read "habits of top founders," forgetting thousands with the same habits who went nowhere. We hear "I mortgaged my house and it worked," while missing the many who did that and went broke. We copy the visible winners, not the invisible base rates. When you only study survivors, you design armor for the wrong places.

Here's how to avoid this reality distortion. Define who you're actually observing—winners, active users, survey responders. Then name who's missing—churned users, failed pilots, silent customers. Finally, rebuild the picture with base rates. Ask: If this were failing, where would I see it? What would break my favorite theory? What's the true probability here? Remember: Success stories have clean arcs. Failures are messy and underreported. Your job isn't to collect better stories—it's to collect better samples. What's unseen can matter more than what's seen. Design for the whole picture, not just the photogenic part.

Give yourself grace.

The “Graceful Goldfish” might be one of the most underrated VeeFriends, and I can’t wait to develop that character more. But this is bigger than a character.

If you’re dealing with something, give yourself grace. You didn’t choose that. You can’t hustle 18 hours a day, 365 days a year. That’s not reality.
If you lost someone you deeply love — a parent, a spouse, God forbid a child — and you’re struggling right now, of course you can’t just “go grind.” If that happened to me, I’m not building VeeFriends the next day. I’m mourning. Please give yourself permission to mourn.

If you’re unpacking old anger, trauma, family pain, addiction in your household growing up... give yourself grace. Don’t live in it forever, but don’t beat yourself up for feeling it either. You can’t go hard if you don’t have fuel.

People ask me what I’m on...It's gratitude. That’s fuel. That’s why I can go 15 hours. I’m not weighed down.

And when I make mistakes — big ones — or wake up on a gloomy day and feel off, I don’t say, “I suck.” You don’t suck either.

Give yourself grace.

A brand we audited cut their Amazon ad spend last month to improve margins. 

The numbers came back worse.

Sales fell. Margin held. Cash flow tightened. Inbound containers were arriving against forecasts that no longer matched the new velocity.

The mistake wasn't running the cut. It was looking at margin in isolation, ignoring inventory turnover and the shipments already in motion.

Here's the thing: Amazon's algorithm runs on velocity.

Lower your spend and your sales velocity usually drops with it. Rank slips. Traffic shifts toward existing customers and away from new discovery. Reviews slow. The flywheel making the listing profitable in the first place loses fuel.

Then your warehouse fills up because the orders you forecasted to inbound inventory don't show up.

A profitable Amazon account is one where ad spend is matched to the velocity the supply chain was built to support.

Cut to fix margin and you usually fix the wrong number.

"We know what works. Early action saves lives, stabilizes communities, and costs far less than responding after catastrophe takes hold. For many people, Somalia may feel distant. But humanitarian catastrophes do not remain contained. Famine fuels displacement across borders, fuels instability in fragile regions, and creates openings for armed groups to exploit desperation. In the Horn of Africa—a region bordering vital shipping lanes-- these effects extend far beyond Somalia itself. 

History is full of moments we only fully understand in hindsight: moments where the warning signs were unmistakable, but action came too late. Somalia is approaching one of those moments now. 

The tools are available. The warning signs are unmistakable. Acting now can still prevent the worst outcomes. Delay will not just increase costs—it will cost lives."

I remember thinking this was the worst thing that had ever happened to me—while also realizing that, as bad as it was at the time, it could have been much worse. This challenge became a teacher, showing me that even our toughest moments can become lessons to serve, give, and lift others. Leaning into my calling, even through pain, reminded me that true energy and momentum come from alignment and gratitude—not lack or comparison. Thank you, Tony, for the reminder to focus on what truly pulls us forward.
